what_happened: A planned job for the steward's base-check request (20261018-070117-qmxv) timed out. Its plan touched 10 files in 4 crates, and the critic accepted it with only minor findings. The operator then split the request into two smaller jobs (20261018-073507-j8rs and 20261018-073510-m3yh) and queued them by hand. This was an intervention, not a job rejection. No acceptance criteria or checks are listed as failed.
cause: Nothing in the pipeline links a plan's size to the producer's fixed deadline. The critic judges a plan on quality (its findings were only minor) and never asks whether one run can finish it. The planning stage also has no step that splits a request into jobs by size. So the first sign of an oversized plan is the producer timing out, after the time is already spent. The operator ends up doing the sizing and splitting by hand. This differs from the reading-scope class, where the user narrows an oversized reading. Here the reading and plan were accepted, and the missing check is on plan size.
prevention: Add a size gate between the critic and the producer. It measures the plan's footprint (files touched, crates touched, and a rough work estimate) against a configured bound that is calibrated from past timeouts. A plan over the bound is not sent to the producer. It goes back to the planner to be split into ordered jobs that each fit the bound. The critic prompt should also list size as a blocking finding. The gate runs in code, so it does not depend on the critic's judgment. A timeout on a planned job should also be recorded against its plan size, so the bound can be tuned.
proposed_request: Make Athena reject oversized plans before the producer runs. After the critic accepts a plan, a code check should count the files and crates the plan touches and compare them with a bound set in athena.toml. The starting bound is 6 files and 2 crates, which sits below the failed plan's 10 files in 4 crates. If a plan is over the bound, Athena should send it back to the planner to split into separate ordered jobs that each fit, and queue those jobs. It should not start the producer on the oversized plan. Also record the plan size on every producer timeout. Done when: a test plan touching 10 files in 4 crates is split into jobs that each fit the bound and none is run whole, and a plan within the bound goes to the producer unchanged.
